Look at the pattern:
${list(seq)}

questnp1-spot#5.af:
Kyk na die patroon:
${list(seq)}

questnp1-spot#6.en: Find the FIRST differences yourself. If they are all the same, it is arithmetic.
questnp1-spot#6.af: Werk self die EERSTE verskille uit. As hulle almal dieselfde is, is dit rekenkundig.

questnp1-spot#7.en: Arithmetic — the first difference is constant.
questnp1-spot#7.af: Rekenkundig: die eerste verskil is konstant.

questnp1-spot#10.en: Every one is ${C(d)}, so the first difference is constant
questnp1-spot#10.af: Elkeen is ${C(d)}, dus is die eerste verskil konstant

questnp1-spot#12.en: Work out the first differences — they change. Their differences (the second differences) are constant → quadratic.
questnp1-spot#12.af: Werk die eerste verskille uit: hulle verander. Hul verskille (die tweede verskille) is konstant → kwadraties.

questnp1-spot#13.en: Quadratic — the second difference is constant.
questnp1-spot#13.af: Kwadraties: die tweede verskil is konstant.

questnp1-spot#14.af: hulle verander, dus nie rekenkundig nie

questnp1-spot#17.en: Divide each term by the one before it (${C(seq[1])} ÷ ${C(seq[0])} = …). A constant ratio means geometric.
questnp1-spot#17.af: Deel elke term deur die vorige een (${C(seq[1])} ÷ ${C(seq[0])} = …). 'n Konstante verhouding beteken dit is meetkundig.

questnp1-spot#18.en: Geometric — you multiply by ${C(r)} each time.
questnp1-spot#18.af: Meetkundig: jy vermenigvuldig elke keer met ${C(r)}.

questnp1-spot#19.en: The differences are not constant, so divide instead
questnp1-spot#19.af: Die verskille is nie konstant nie, deel dus eerder

questnp1-spot#23.en: For the quadratic pattern ${list(seq)}, which differences are constant?
questnp1-spot#23.af: In die kwadratiese patroon ${list(seq)}, watter verskille is konstant?

questnp1-spot#28.en: Work out the first differences (they change), then their differences (those stay the same).
questnp1-spot#28.af: Werk die eerste verskille uit (hulle verander), en dan hul verskille (dié bly dieselfde).

questnp1-spot#31.en: all the same → this is the constant row
questnp1-spot#31.af: almal dieselfde → dit is die konstante ry

questnp1-spot#32.en: What is the constant first difference of ${list(seq)}?
questnp1-spot#32.af: Wat is die konstante eerste verskil van ${list(seq)}?

questnp1-spot#33.en: Subtract any term from the one after it (next − previous).
questnp1-spot#33.af: Trek enige term van die volgende een af (volgende − vorige).

questnp1-spot#37.en: same, so the difference is constant
questnp1-spot#37.af: dieselfde, dus is die verskil konstant

questnp1-spot#38.en: Tap the first difference between T₂ and T₃ (the middle of the top difference row).
questnp1-spot#38.af: Klik op die eerste verskil tussen T₂ en T₃ (die middel van die boonste verskilry).

questnp1-spot#39.en: First differences sit between two terms. The one between the 2nd and 3rd terms is the middle cell.
questnp1-spot#39.af: Eerste verskille staan tussen twee terme. Die een tussen die 2de en 3de terme is die middelste sel.

questnp1-spot#40.en: Look at the top difference row: its middle cell sits between T₂ and T₃.
questnp1-spot#40.af: Kyk na die boonste verskilry: die middelste sel staan tussen T₂ en T₃.

questnp1-spot#42.en: A first difference sits between two terms
questnp1-spot#42.af: 'n Eerste verskil staan tussen twee terme

questnp1-spot#46.en: By what do you multiply to move along ${list(seq)}?
questnp1-spot#46.af: Waarmee vermenigvuldig jy elke keer in die patroon ${list(seq)}?

questnp1-spot#47.en: Divide a term by the one before it.
questnp1-spot#47.af: Deel 'n term deur die vorige een.

questnp2-arithmetic#2.en: d = any term minus the term before it.

questnp2-arithmetic#7.en: same, so d is the common difference

questnp2-arithmetic#8.en: What is the next term of ${list(seq)}?

questnp2-arithmetic#9.en: Add the common difference (${C(d)}) to the last term.

questnp2-arithmetic#13.en: Find the general term Tₙ of ${list(seq)}.

questnp2-arithmetic#14.en: Tₙ = an + c: a is the constant difference (so start with that many n), and c = T₀ — step BACK one difference from T₁.

questnp2-arithmetic#15.en: a = ${C(d)} and c = T₀ = ${C(a1)} − ${P(d)} = ${C(c)}, so Tₙ = ${correct}.

questnp2-arithmetic#19.en: step BACK one difference from T₁

questnp2-arithmetic#22.en: First build Tₙ = an + c: a = the difference (${C(d)}), c = T₀ = ${C(a1)} − ${P(d)} = ${C(a1 - d)}. Then put n = ${C(n)} in.

questnp2-arithmetic#29.en: A pattern has Tₙ = ${form}. Find T${C(n)}.

questnp2-arithmetic#35.en: In ${list(seq)} ; …, which term is equal to ${C(value)}? (Find n.)

questnp2-arithmetic#36.en: Build Tₙ = an + c first (a = ${C(d)}, c = T₀ = ${C(a1 - d)}), then set it equal to ${C(value)} and solve for n.

questnp2-arithmetic#40.en: Set it equal to the value: ${form} = ${C(value)}

questnp2-arithmetic#43.en: In the form Tₙ = an + c, what does c equal?

questnp2-arithmetic#44.en: T₀ — the term that would sit before T₁

questnp2-arithmetic#48.en: Put n = 0 into an + c. You get c — the ‘zero-th’ term, one step before T₁.

questnp2-arithmetic#49.en: c = T₀ (and a is the common difference).

questnp3-quadratic#1.en: What is the constant second difference of ${list(seq)}?

questnp3-quadratic#2.en: Take the differences of the first differences (bottom row of the pyramid).

questnp3-quadratic#8.en: They are all ${C(sd)}, so the second difference is ${C(sd)}

questnp3-quadratic#9.en: For ${list(seq)}, use 2a = second difference to find a.

questnp3-quadratic#10.en: Read the second difference off the pyramid, then halve it.

questnp3-quadratic#16.en: For ${list(seq)}, with a = ${C(a)}, use 3a + b = T₂ − T₁ to find b.

questnp3-quadratic#17.en: 3a + b = T₂ − T₁. So b = (T₂ − T₁) − 3a = ${C(seq[1] - seq[0])} − 3(${C(a)}).

questnp3-quadratic#23.en: For ${list(seq)}, with a = ${C(a)} and b = ${C(b)}, use a + b + c = T₁ to find c.

questnp3-quadratic#27.en: put n = 1 into an² + bn + c

questnp3-quadratic#30.en: Find the general term Tₙ of ${list(seq)}.

questnp3-quadratic#31.en: Find a, then b, then c with the three relationships, and write an² + bn + c.

questnp3-quadratic#38.en: A pattern has Tₙ = ${quadStr(a, b, c)}. Find T${C(n)}.

questnp3-quadratic#39.en: Substitute n = ${C(n)} (square it first): a(${C(n)})² + b(${C(n)}) + c.

questnp4-missing#7.en: This is a quadratic pattern. Find the missing term x.

questnp4-missing#9.en: Write the first differences (some contain x), then set the two second differences EQUAL and solve for x.

questnp4-missing#10.en: Keeping the second difference constant gives x = ${C(answer)} (full pattern: ${list(seq)}).

questnp4-missing#11.en: Form the first differences around x, then make the two second differences equal.

questnp4-missing#13.en: A quadratic pattern starts T₁ = ${C(t1)}, T₂ = ${C(t2)}, and its constant second difference is ${C(sd)}. Find T₃.

questnp4-missing#14.en: Next first difference = (T₂ − T₁) + second difference = ${C(t2 - t1)} + ${P(sd)}. Add that to T₂.

questnp4-missing#17.en: Next gap = first gap + second difference = ${C(t2 - t1)} + ${P(sd)} = ${C(t2 - t1 + sd)}

questnp4-missing#19.en: T₃ = T₂ + next gap = ${C(t2)} + ${P(t2 - t1 + sd)} = ${C(seq[2])}

questnp4-missing#20.en: To find a missing term in a quadratic pattern, which value do you keep constant?

questnp4-missing#25.en: Quadratic ⇒ the SECOND difference is the same throughout.

questnp4-missing#27.en: In a quadratic number pattern, are the second differences always equal to each other?

questnp4-missing#28.en: That constant second difference is exactly what makes a pattern quadratic.

questnp4-missing#29.en: Yes — a constant second difference is the defining feature.

questnp5-minmax#1.en: The pattern Tₙ = ${quadStr(a, b, c)} has a turning point. Is it a minimum or a maximum?

questnp5-minmax#6.en: a > 0 → ‘happy’ parabola → minimum.  a < 0 → ‘sad’ parabola → maximum.

questnp5-minmax#8.en: The coefficient of n² is a = ${C(a)}

questnp5-minmax#9.en: look at the n² term only

questnp5-minmax#14.en: For Tₙ = ${quadStr(a, b, c)}, which term n is the turning point? Use n = −b ÷ (2a).

questnp5-minmax#18.en: read them off Tₙ = an² + bn + c

questnp5-minmax#21.en: For Tₙ = ${quadStr(a, b, c)}, which term n has the ${kind} value? (n must be a whole number.)

questnp5-minmax#22.en: Work out n = −b ÷ (2a). It is NOT a whole number — a term number must be, so take the nearest whole n.

questnp5-minmax#23.en: n = ${C(-b)} ÷ ${P(2 * a)} = ${C(nStar)} — not a whole number, so the ${kind} term is the nearest: n = ${C(k)}.

questnp5-minmax#25.en: A term number must be a natural number → nearest whole n = ${C(k)}

questnp5-minmax#26.en: T${toSub(k)} = ${C(quadTn(a, b, c)(k))} is the ${kind} term

questnp5-minmax#34.en: Tₙ plotted against n · each grid block is 1

questnp5-minmax#35.en: Follow the dashed line from the turning point down to the horizontal axis and count the blocks from 0.

questnp5-minmax#36.en: The turning point is at n = ${C(k)}.

questnp5-minmax#37.en: The turning point is the ${a > 0 ? "lowest" : "highest"} point of the curve

questnp5-minmax#39.en: Follow it straight down to the n-axis and count the blocks from 0:  n = ${C(k)}

questnp5-minmax#40.en: The graph shows the terms of a pattern. What is the value of the turning point?

questnp5-minmax#41.en: Count the grid blocks from the horizontal axis (each block is 1) up or down to the turning point.

questnp5-minmax#43.en: Count the blocks from the n-axis ${value < 0 ? "down" : "up"} to it (each block is 1):  Tₙ = ${C(value)}

questnp5-minmax#44.en: A number pattern has a minimum term when…

questnp5-minmax#45.en: a > 0 (the coefficient of n² is positive)

questnp5-minmax#46.en: a < 0 (the coefficient of n² is negative)

questnp5-minmax#49.en: Same rule as a parabola: a positive ‘opens up’, so the turning point is the lowest point.

questnp5-minmax#50.en: When a > 0 (positive n² coefficient) the turning point is a minimum.

questnp6-gaps#1.en: For the quadratic pattern ${list(seq)} ; …, find the gap between T${C(k)} and T${C(k + 1)}, that is T${C(k + 1)} − T${C(k)}.

questnp6-gaps#2.en: The gaps form a linear pattern: first gap = ${C(g1)}, changing by ${C(sd)} each time. Build gapₙ = an + c: a = ${C(sd)}, c = gap₀ = ${C(g1)} − ${P(sd)} = ${C(gapC0(g1, sd))}. Then put n = ${C(k)} in.

questnp6-gaps#3.en: gapₙ = ${gapForm(g1, sd)}, so gap ${C(k)} = ${gapForm(g1, sd).replace("n", `(${C(k)})`)} = ${C(gapAt(g1, sd, k))}.

questnp6-gaps#4.en: The gaps are ${list(firstDiffs(seq))} — an arithmetic pattern

questnp6-gaps#6.en: a = ${C(sd)} and c = gap₀ = ${C(g1)} − ${P(sd)} = ${C(gapC0(g1, sd))}  →  gapₙ = ${gapForm(g1, sd)}

questnp6-gaps#9.en: the gap between T${C(k)} and T${C(k + 1)}

questnp6-gaps#11.en: Build gapₙ = an + c first (a = ${C(sd)}, c = gap₀ = ${C(gapC0(g1, sd))}), then set it equal to ${C(value)} and solve for n.

questnp6-gaps#12.en: n = ${C(n)} (the gap between T${C(n)} and T${C(n + 1)}).

questnp6-gaps#13.en: The gaps are arithmetic: a = ${C(sd)}, c = gap₀ = ${C(g1)} − ${P(sd)} = ${C(gapC0(g1, sd))}

questnp6-gaps#16.en: the gap between T${C(n)} and T${C(n + 1)}

questnp6-gaps#29.en: That is exactly the constant second difference.

questnp6-gaps#30.en: The gaps change by ${C(sd)} each time (the second difference).

questnp6-gaps#32.en: that is the constant second difference

questnp7-geometric#2.en: Divide any term by the term before it.

questnp7-geometric#17.en: Tₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹ with a = T₁ and r the ratio. Keep a and r separate.

questnp7-geometric#22.en: keep a and r apart — the power sits on r only

questnp7-geometric#24.en: Tₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹ = ${C(a1)} × ${C(r)}^(${C(k)} − 1). Do the power first.

questnp7-geometric#30.en: power first, then multiply by a

questnp7-geometric#32.en: Dividing by ${C(div)} is the same as multiplying by 1 over ${C(div)}.

questnp7-geometric#34.en: Dividing by ${C(div)} is the same as multiplying by 1/${C(div)}

questnp7-geometric#37.en: In Tₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹, should you multiply a and r together before raising to the power?

questnp7-geometric#38.en: Order of operations: powers before multiplication. Do rⁿ⁻¹ first, THEN multiply by a.

questnp7-geometric#39.en: No — raise r to the power first, then multiply by a.
